坐或站，將鼓置於身前合適位置。將鼓穩定放置於地面或夾於雙腿之間。用手掌或鼓棒敲擊: Sit or stand with the drum in front of you at a comfortable height. Rest it firmly on the ground or hold it between your legs. Strike the centre or the edge of the head with the palm or a drumstick; different places give different timbres. How hard you strike decides the volume. The sound is made by striking, so watch where you strike and how much force you use.

納卡拉鼓屬中東壺鼓系統，名稱源自烏爾都語中「敲擊」義的動詞。阿拔斯後期與法蒂瑪王: The naqara belongs to the Middle Eastern kettle-drum family, and its name comes from an Urdu verb meaning to strike. In the late Abbasid period and under the Fatimids the drums were struck before the five daily prayers; Iran once kept drum houses where they announced sunrise, victories and other news. In India they were used in the ensemble of nine instruments, and later they often accompanied the Indian oboe. They reached Europe in the thirteenth century, after the Crusades, through Saracen musicians, and the French, Italian and English names all come from this; they arrived in England in the fourteenth century and were used when Edward III entered Calais in 1347, faded after the seventeenth century, and the later timpani developed from them.
納卡拉鼓屬膜鳴樂器中的鍋鼓類型，來源載明圓背部分以燒製黏土製成，鼓面為處理過的獸: The naqara is of the kettle-drum type among membranophones: the source states that the round back is made of fired clay, that the head is treated hide, and that it is fixed to the rim with rope and drawn tight over the bowl-shaped back. The desarkutan of northern Iran has a clay body covered with cowhide — wild boar hide in the past — tensioned with straps made from cattle tendon. The Georgian diplipito is two clay pots covered with leather; the Uzbek koshnaqara is a pair of clay pots with goatskin heads. It is played with a short wooden stick; the materials of the other parts are not stated.

They are also heard in Turkish Ottoman mehter military music, in medieval European military, chamber, dance and processional music, and in Georgian vocal and dance ensembles, combining with instruments such as the duduki, buzika, panduri and salamuri.

The naqara is a membranophone of the Middle East, Asia and Europe, of the kettle-drum kind: its round back is made of fired clay, its flat face is covered with treated hide, fixed with rope around the edge and drawn tight over the bowl. It is usually played in pairs, one drum low and one high, struck with short, out-curved wooden mallets. It appears in Iraqi maqam ensembles, at festivals and weddings in northern Iran, in India's naubat ensemble of nine instruments and at North Indian weddings, and in Turkish Ottoman military music; it is also used in European military music, chamber music, dance and processional music, and in Georgian folk ensembles.
納卡拉鼓音色明亮而富有穿透力，具有清晰的金屬質感和鏗鏘之音。其音域偏高，能夠在樂: The naqara has a bright, penetrating timbre with a clear metallic ring and a clanging attack. Its range sits high, so it stands out in an ensemble. The drums are usually used in pairs, tuned by different head tensions to two close but slightly differing pitches, which gives a rich, resonant harmony. When the mallets strike the hide head the sound projects well, and its quick decay gives it a strong rhythmic feel. Compared with the heavy, low sound of Western timpani, the naqara is lighter and sharper; compared with cymbals it carries far more definite pitch. Its resonance is shaped by the round copper or clay body, which gives it a distinctive Eastern colour, and in Middle Eastern music it marks out the rhythm and lifts the atmosphere.
